data.title: CRX-90 Communication Matrix
data.solution:
from math import ceil
h = int(input())
w = int(input())
n = int(input())
turns = [*map(int,input().split())]
grid = []
for _ in ' '*h:
    grid += [input()]

cr = (h-1)//2
cc = (w-1)//2

hori = grid[cr]
vert = []
for i in range(h):
    vert += [grid[i][cc]]

# row transformation model
overlap_base = hori
if len(vert) > len(hori):
    overlap_base = overlap_base.center(len(vert), ' ')
cc = (len(overlap_base)-1)//2 # Patch

# Rotate 90 Clockwise - +1
overlap = ''
for i in range(h-1,-1,-1):
    vert_seat = vert[i]
    alpha = i-cr
    hori_seat = overlap_base[cc-alpha]
    if vert_seat == hori_seat:
        overlap += vert_seat
    elif vert_seat == ' ' or hori_seat == ' ':
        overlap += (vert_seat+hori_seat).strip()
    elif vert_seat != hori_seat:
        overlap += ' '
overlap = overlap_base[:cc+1-ceil(len(overlap)/2)] + overlap + overlap_base[cc+ceil(len(overlap)/2):]

# Rotate 90 Anticlockwise - -1
overlap_rev = ''
for i in range(h):
    vert_seat = vert[i]
    alpha = i-cr
    hori_seat = overlap_base[cc+alpha]
    if vert_seat == hori_seat:
        overlap_rev += vert_seat
    elif vert_seat == ' ' or hori_seat == ' ':
        overlap_rev += (vert_seat+hori_seat).strip()
    elif vert_seat != hori_seat:
        overlap_rev += ' '
overlap_rev = overlap_base[:cc+1-ceil(len(overlap_rev)/2)] + overlap_rev + overlap_base[cc+ceil(len(overlap_rev)/2):]    

# States
'''
hor - horizontal row
vert - vertical coloumn
overlap_base - formatted horizontal row with space to even out
overlap - Overlap Condition +1
overlap_rev - Overlap Condition -1
'''
states = [hori, overlap, hori, overlap_rev]

global_turn = 0
for turn in turns:
    global_turn = (global_turn + turn)%4
    print(states[global_turn])
data.statement:
The CRX (Cross Routing eXchanger) Communication Matrix is a multilayer routing module used in high-density communication systems. It consists of horizontal and vertical strips arranged in multiple layers, where each strip can independently rotate in <<multiples of 90°>> to dynamically modulate communication channels.

Each position on a strip is in one of three states:

{{A}} — Channel {{A}}, which carries only Type-<<A>> signals.
{{B}} — Channel {{B}}, which carries only Type-<<B>> signals.
{{Whitespace}} — An <<Open Channel>>, through which signals of any type may pass.

During normal operation, every strip is controlled automatically by the synchronization system. During a maintenance cycle, however, engineers are given manual control over only the front-center strip. The remaining strips continue operating automatically and are outside the scope of this simulation.

The center horizontal strip is permanently fixed and serves as the matrix's diagnostic bus. The front-center strip rotates about its own center in <<multiples of 90°>>. Whenever its orientation becomes horizontal, it overlaps the diagnostic bus, and the states of the two strips combine according to the following routing rules:

{{Whitespace}} + {{Whitespace}} → {{Whitespace}}
{{A}} + {{B}} or {{B}} + {{A}} → {{Whitespace}}
{{A}} + {{A}} → {{A}}
{{B}} + {{B}} → {{B}}
{{Whitespace}} + <<X>> or <<X>> + {{Whitespace}} → <<X>>, where <<X>> represents either {{A}} or {{B}}.

<<These rules have the following interpretation>>:
An <<Open Channel>> allows any signal to pass.
Channel {{A}} and Channel {{B}} are complementary. When they overlap, they form an <<Open Channel>>, allowing all signal types to pass.
Identical channels are incompatible and therefore remain unchanged.
An <<Open Channel>> contributes no restriction, so the other channel remains visible.

<<For each maintenance round>>:
A <<positive value>> rotates the front-center strip 90° <<clockwise per unit>>.
A <<negative value>> rotates it 90° <<counterclockwise per unit>>.

After applying the specified rotation, output the current state of the diagnostic bus (the center horizontal row).

The communication matrix <<does not reset>> between maintenance rounds. Each round begins from the panel's current state.

If the rotated strip extends beyond the diagnostic bus, <<output the additional cells>> exactly as they appear on the rotated strip.

<<Example:>>
```
turns = "+1 +1"

   A
   B
   A
   B
AABABAA    -- +1 turn --> BAA ABA A
   A
    
   A
   B


                               B
                               A
                                
                               A
BAA ABA A   -- +1 turn -->  AABABAA
                               B
                               A
                               B
                               A
                                   (reversed)

Output - 
BAA ABABA
AABABAA
```

lastVersion.statementHTML:
Goal

The CRX (Cross Routing eXchanger) Communication Matrix is a multilayer routing module used in high-density communication systems. It consists of horizontal and vertical strips arranged in multiple layers, where each strip can independently rotate in multiples of 90° to dynamically modulate communication channels.

Each position on a strip is in one of three states:

A — Channel A, which carries only Type-A signals.
B — Channel B, which carries only Type-B signals.
Whitespace — An Open Channel, through which signals of any type may pass.

During normal operation, every strip is controlled automatically by the synchronization system. During a maintenance cycle, however, engineers are given manual control over only the front-center strip. The remaining strips continue operating automatically and are outside the scope of this simulation.

The center horizontal strip is permanently fixed and serves as the matrix's diagnostic bus. The front-center strip rotates about its own center in multiples of 90°. Whenever its orientation becomes horizontal, it overlaps the diagnostic bus, and the states of the two strips combine according to the following routing rules:

Whitespace + Whitespace → Whitespace
A + B or B + A → Whitespace
A + A → A
B + B → B
Whitespace + X or X + Whitespace → X, where X represents either A or B.

These rules have the following interpretation:
An Open Channel allows any signal to pass.
Channel A and Channel B are complementary. When they overlap, they form an Open Channel, allowing all signal types to pass.
Identical channels are incompatible and therefore remain unchanged.
An Open Channel contributes no restriction, so the other channel remains visible.

For each maintenance round:
A positive value rotates the front-center strip 90° clockwise per unit.
A negative value rotates it 90° counterclockwise per unit.

After applying the specified rotation, output the current state of the diagnostic bus (the center horizontal row).

The communication matrix does not reset between maintenance rounds. Each round begins from the panel's current state.

If the rotated strip extends beyond the diagnostic bus, output the additional cells exactly as they appear on the rotated strip.

Example:

turns = "+1 +1"

   A
   B
   A
   B
AABABAA    -- +1 turn --> BAA ABA A
   A
    
   A
   B


                               B
                               A
                                
                               A
BAA ABA A   -- +1 turn -->  AABABAA
                               B
                               A
                               B
                               A
                                   (reversed)

Output - 
BAA ABABA
AABABAA





   

      
Input

      
Line 1: An odd integer h, the height of the communication matrix.
Line 2: An odd integer w, the width of the communication matrix.
Line 3: An integer n, the number of maintenance rounds.
Line 4: n signed integers separated by spaces, representing the rotations for each maintenance round.
Next h Lines: A string of length w, representing one row of the communication matrix.

   

   

      
Output

      
For each maintenance round: Output the resulting state of the diagnostic bus (the center horizontal row).

   

   

      
Constraints

      
The matrix always has exactly one center row and one center column.
Rotations are always multiples of 90°.
The remaining strips continue operating automatically and are outside the scope of this simulation

   

   

      
Example

      

         

            
Input

            
9
7
2
+1 +1
BBBABB 
A ABAAA
ABBAABA
B BBA B
AABABAA
BBBAAAB
AAB BBB
BABAABA
B ABAB 

         

         

            
Output

            
BAA ABA A
AABABAA
